questions.q: In the Linux kernel, what exactly is a 'container'?
choices: A special kernel object created by a dedicated create_container() system call
An ordinary process placed into namespaces and cgroups, usually with its own root filesystem
A lightweight virtual machine with its own emulated kernel
A feature provided only by Docker that the kernel itself knows nothing about until Docker is installed
questions.explain: There is no 'container' object in the kernel and no create_container() call. A container is just a normal process that the kernel has put into namespaces (changing what it can see) and cgroups (limiting what it can use), usually with a swapped-in root filesystem. Docker, Podman, and Kubernetes are orchestration glue over those primitives.

questions.q: Why is the user namespace considered the security keystone of containers?
choices: It encrypts all traffic leaving the container
It limits how much CPU and memory the container can consume
It maps in-container UID 0 (root) to an unprivileged UID on the host, so a breakout does not hand over real root
It hides the host's process list from the container
questions.explain: Inside a user namespace a process can be 'root' (UID 0) internally while mapping to a powerless high UID on the host. So even a container breakout lands the attacker as nobody, not host root. This is exactly what makes rootless containers (Podman, rootless Docker) safe.

questions.q: cgroups v2 are used to do what for a container?
choices: Give it a private network stack with its own interfaces and routes
Limit and account the resources it uses, such as CPU, memory, I/O, and process count
Provide it with a separate root filesystem to live in
Make its first process appear as PID 1
questions.explain: Namespaces isolate visibility; cgroups limit resources. cgroup v2 caps CPU, memory, I/O, and PIDs through a filesystem interface — you literally write numbers into files like cpu.max and memory.max. That is what 'docker run --cpus' and '--memory' do under the hood.

questions.q: What is the difference between 'unshare' and 'nsenter'?
choices: 'unshare' creates new namespaces to build a container; 'nsenter' enters the existing namespaces of a running process to debug it
'unshare' limits CPU usage; 'nsenter' limits memory usage
'unshare' is for Docker only; 'nsenter' is for Podman only
They are aliases for the same command with no real difference
questions.explain: They are mirror images. 'unshare' makes brand-new namespaces and runs a process inside them — that is how you build a container by hand. 'nsenter' joins the namespaces a process is already in — perfect for debugging a running container, even one too minimal to have its own shell.

questions.q: Inside a container with its own PID namespace, your application runs as PID 1. Why does 'docker run --init' inject a tiny init such as tini?
choices: Because containers cannot start without a process named 'tini'
Because PID 1 must reap orphaned zombies and forward signals, and most apps were not written to do that job
Because tini decrypts the container image before it runs
Because the kernel refuses to assign PID 1 to anything but a dedicated init binary
questions.explain: PID 1 has special duties: reaping zombie children and forwarding signals like SIGTERM. An ordinary app running as PID 1 usually does neither, so 'docker stop' ends up SIGKILLing it ungracefully and zombies pile up. '--init' drops in a small, correct init (tini or dumb-init) to handle those duties — the same PID-1 responsibility from ordinary Linux, surfacing in a container.
